draft.title: Asking historical questions
card: Historians start with a question. It sets what they want to find out about the past.
A good question is open. Questions that start with why or how need an explanation. A closed question, such as "When did it happen?", has a short answer and leads nowhere further.
A good question can be answered from evidence. Sources from the time, such as objects, buildings and writing, must exist or be likely to be found.
A good question also guides the search. It tells you which sources to look for and what to look for in them.
draft.remember: A good historical question is open, can be answered with evidence, and points to the sources you need.

a.q: Which of these is the best historical question to start an investigation?
opts: How did people in ancient Egypt build the pyramids?
In what year was the Great Pyramid finished?
Was ancient Egypt a better place than ancient Greece?
What did ancient Egyptians dream about at night?
a.why: The how question is open and can be answered from evidence such as tools, quarries and building remains. The year question is closed and has a short answer. The dreams question is open but there is almost no evidence to answer it.
a.clue: Look for a question that is open and has evidence to answer it.

b.q: Priya is studying a rock shelter in Queensland with old paintings on its walls. Which question would best guide her search for sources?
opts: Why did people make paintings at this shelter?
How many paintings are at this shelter?
Did the people who painted here enjoy it?
Are the paintings here the best in Australia?
b.why: The why question is open, and it points Priya to sources such as the paintings, other objects found nearby, and the knowledge held by the traditional owners. The count question is closed and a single number answers it. The enjoyment question cannot be answered from evidence.
b.clue: Pick the question that is open and tells her where to look.

a.best: How did people in ancient Egypt build the pyramids?

b.best: Why did people make paintings at this shelter?

problems.detail: The card says questions that start with how need an explanation, but question b uses "How many paintings are at this shelter?" as a closed question. A Year 7 student following the card's rule could be confused. The card should note that "how many" or "how long" questions can be closed.

"A closed question... has a short answer and leads nowhere further" overstates it. Historians often use closed questions as supporting questions inside an inquiry. Better: closed questions alone do not lead to an explanation.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, and the explanations match them. The card's rule that 'how' questions are open clashes with the closed 'How many' option, and it overstates that closed questions lead nowhere. Question b involves Aboriginal rock art and handles it respectfully.

proposal.title: Asking historical questions
card: A historian's inquiry starts with a question. A good one is open: it needs an explanation, such as why or how something happened.
A closed question, such as "When did it happen?" or "How many are there?", has a short answer. It can help as a smaller step, but on its own it does not lead to an explanation.
A good question can be answered from evidence, such as objects, buildings and writing. Questions about private feelings or dreams, or which place was best, cannot be settled by evidence.
A good question also guides the search. It tells you which sources to look for and what to look for in them.
proposal.remember: A good historical question is open, can be answered with evidence, and points to the sources you need.

a.q: Which of these is the best historical question to start an investigation?
opts: How did people in ancient Egypt build the pyramids?
In what year was the Great Pyramid finished?
Was ancient Egypt a better place than ancient Greece?
What did ancient Egyptians dream about at night?
a.why: The pyramids question asks how something happened, so it needs an explanation, and tools, quarries and building remains can answer it. The year question is closed and has a short answer. The dreams question cannot be answered from evidence, and which place was better is a judgement evidence cannot settle.
a.clue: Look for a question that needs an explanation and has evidence to answer it.

b.q: Priya is studying a rock shelter in Queensland with old paintings on its walls. Which question would best guide her search for sources?
opts: Why did people make paintings at this shelter?
How many paintings are at this shelter?
Did the people who painted here enjoy it?
Are the paintings here the best in Australia?
b.why: The why question is open, and it points Priya to sources such as the paintings, objects found nearby, and the knowledge held by the Traditional Owners. The how many question starts with how, but it is closed: a single number answers it. Enjoyment is a private feeling, and which paintings are best is a judgement, so evidence cannot settle either.
b.clue: A question starting with how can still have a one-number answer.
